name: Fredrikstad
title: Hull Gauging Fredrikstad: Ships at the Port of Borg on the Glomma
description: Hull thickness measurement in Fredrikstad and the Port of Borg for bulk, forest-product, container and ro-ro ships: holds, tanks, decks and piping.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Cargo Ships at Fredrikstad and the Port of Borg
intro: Fredrikstad lies at the mouth of the Glomma, Norway's longest river, where the Port of Borg serves Fredrikstad, Greaker and Sarpsborg from berths along the river. Bulk carriers, forest-product ships, container feeders, ro-ro and reefer ships come up through the Hvaler archipelago to load and discharge for the industries of Østfold. Calls here are working cargo calls, and gauging fits around them. Every job is done by technicians who fly from India to the ship; there is no Atlantis presence in Østfold.

highlights.p: Ships at Fredrikstad and Sarpsborg lie alongside in the river, well away from the open sea. The protected berths make hull access from the quay, gangway work and deck measurements far less dependent on weather than at exposed coastal ports, even in autumn and winter.

Forest-product cargoes need dry, clean holds, and condensation or water leaking past worn hatch covers is what damages both cargo and steel. Hold plating, hatch covers and coamings are best gauged in the gap between discharge and the next loading, while the holds are empty.

Liquid bulk berths serve industry along the Glomma, and product and chemical tankers calling there can have ballast tanks, deck structure and engine-room piping measured while they discharge. Cargo tanks stay closed, and the terminal's safety rules apply to everything done on deck.

port.h: Fredrikstad, the Glomma and the Port of Borg
p: Fredrikstad sits on both banks of the Glomma close to where Norway's longest river meets the outer Oslofjord, on its eastern side not far from the Swedish border. Ships reach the city from the Skagerrak through the sounds of the Hvaler archipelago and then up the river channel, with pilots aboard for the confined approach. The Port of Borg is an inter-municipal port whose main areas are at Fredrikstad, Greaker and Sarpsborg, the last two further upriver towards the industrial town of Sarpsborg. Size limits are set by the river and its berths, so the ships here are short-sea and smaller deep-sea tonnage rather than large ocean-going bulk carriers. The river carries a strong outflow, particularly during the spring flood when snowmelt from the inland valleys reaches the sea, and berthing is planned with that current in mind.

Cargo at Borg is broad for a port of its size: dry and liquid bulk, forest products, ro-ro, reefer cargo, breakbulk and containers, with cruise ships occasionally using the cargo berths. Feeder container ships connect the port with the continental hubs, ro-ro and general cargo ships carry industrial goods, and bulk ships bring raw materials for the region's plants. Sarpsborg's industry, including the Borregaard biorefinery, and plants in Fredrikstad such as the titanium dioxide works depend on sea transport for part of their supply. Product and chemical tankers serve the liquid bulk installations. Fredrikstad was for much of the twentieth century a major shipbuilding town; its large yard closed in the 1980s and the site has since been redeveloped, so the ships calling today take their dockings elsewhere.

Gauging windows at Fredrikstad are the cargo stays themselves. A feeder works its containers in hours; a bulk or forest-product ship may spend a day or more loading or discharging, with holds freeing up one by one; a tanker discharges over a shift or two. Ships waiting for cargo or for a berth sometimes lie at a quay or at anchor outside the river. Winters in Østfold are colder than on the west coast, and a severe cold spell can bring ice to the river and the inner sounds, which slows traffic and makes outside work harder; in most winters the port operates normally. The spring flood and autumn rain send fast, brown river water past the berths but rarely affect work aboard, which is one advantage a river port has over an exposed harbour.

facilities.h: Where gauging fits at Fredrikstad, Greaker and Sarpsborg
p: All three port areas offer quay-side work on ships during cargo operations. At the bulk and general cargo berths, holds are gauged as they are cleared, with tank-tops, hopper plating and lower frames first and upper structure where access allows. At the container berth, scrubber pipework, deck plating and void spaces are measured while the terminal works the ship. Tankers at the liquid bulk berths allow ballast tanks, deck structure and engine-room piping to be measured, with the cargo tanks closed and the terminal's safety rules applied to everything on deck.

Ships calling at Borg normally dock at yards on the Norwegian, Swedish or Danish coasts, in Poland or further afield, according to the owner's contracts, and readings taken during a Fredrikstad call are commonly used to build the steel estimate for that docking. Where a ship lies idle at a quay between cargoes, or is laid up in the area, ballast tank and double-bottom entry becomes practical and a fuller condition survey can be done. The river berths are close to the city, which keeps the team's daily travel between hotel and ship short.
list: Fredrikstad bulk and general cargo berths — tank-top, hopper and frame gauging as holds are cleared during discharge or loading.
Container berth — scrubber wash-water lines, deck plating and void spaces on feeder ships while cargo is worked.
Greaker and Sarpsborg industrial berths — hold and ballast tank readings on bulk ships serving the plants upriver.
Liquid bulk berths — ballast tank, deck and engine-room piping measurements on product and chemical tankers, cargo tanks closed.
Ro-ro and reefer berths — car-deck, ramp and reefer-hold structure checks during cargo stays.
Quays used for lay-by — fuller condition surveys on ships waiting between cargoes.

context.h: Port state control and cargo-driven corrosion on the Glomma
p: Ships at the Port of Borg come under Paris MoU port state control, carried out by the Norwegian Maritime Authority, and the mix of short-sea general cargo ships and older bulk tonnage means structural deficiencies are a regular subject of inspection, with wasted hatch coamings, holed air pipes and corroded deck fittings high on the list. When an inspector requires readings or a repair before departure, the owner needs a team quickly, and if visas or the ship's movements rule out Fredrikstad, the practical answer is often to measure at the next port or the docking yard. Ships of 500 gross tonnage and above that trade to the EU must keep an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, which weighs on the older ships in this trade as they near the end of their careers.

Cargo shapes the corrosion picture. Forest-product ships suffer from condensation and from water entering through hatch covers whose seals or coamings are worn, which wets the holds as well as the cargo, so gauging of covers, coamings and hold plating addresses the cause. Bulk raw materials for chemical plants can be abrasive or chemically aggressive when damp, and residues trapped at bilge wells and tank-top edges drive local wastage. Tankers bring the usual ballast tank and scrubber questions. Water at the river berths is fresh or brackish rather than full-strength seawater; that does not change the gauging scope, but ballast taken on in the river can carry silt into the tanks, and silt deposits hide pitting until they are washed out.

jobs.h: Typical gauging work at the Port of Borg
jobs.p: Fredrikstad jobs are usually short scopes on working ships, booked once the call is fixed. The superintendent tells us which spaces matter, the ship prepares access and lighting, and the team measures during cargo operations without asking the terminal to change its plan. For ships with longer stays or idle days, ballast tanks and double bottoms can be added. Reports follow the ship's thickness measurement plan so the readings can go straight into the survey history and the yard specification. Where the call is too short for the full scope, we say so plainly and propose finishing the work at the next port or at the docking. Requests we typically see include:
list: Hold tank-top, hopper and lower-frame gauging on a bulk ship discharging raw materials for a plant upriver.
Hatch cover, coaming and hold plating readings on a forest-product ship, with corroded areas around the compression bars recorded.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard pipe measurements on a container feeder during cargo work.
Ballast tank, deck and engine-room piping gauging on a chemical tanker at the liquid bulk berth, cargo tanks kept closed.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of a short-sea general cargo ship lying at a Fredrikstad quay between cargoes.

logistics: Oslo Airport at Gardermoen is the usual arrival point, with trains via Oslo on the Østfold line to Fredrikstad and Sarpsborg. Quay access at Fredrikstad, Greaker and Sarpsborg is controlled under ISPS and arranged through the ship's agent, with plant inductions where a berth belongs to an industrial site. Norway sits inside the Schengen area, so the team travels from India on Schengen visas, and owners should send us the call dates as soon as they are fixed so the applications can start in time.

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged while it lies at a river berth in Fredrikstad?
faqs.a: Yes. The river berths are sheltered, so hull access from the quay, gangway work and deck measurement go ahead in most weather. Holds are gauged as they are cleared during cargo operations, and ballast tanks can be added if the ship can empty, ventilate and certify them for entry. The main limit is the length of the call, not the conditions.

faqs.q: Where do ships calling at the Port of Borg go for dry-docking?
faqs.a: Wherever the owner holds a contract: yards on the Norwegian, Swedish and Danish coasts are common for short-sea ships, and larger ships go to Poland, Turkey or Asia. Readings taken during a Fredrikstad call give that yard an early steel estimate. If the owner wishes, the same team can then travel on to the docking yard to finish the renewal survey gauging with the class surveyor present.

faqs.q: Does winter ice stop work at Fredrikstad?
faqs.a: Rarely. The port normally operates through the winter, though a severe cold spell can bring ice to the river and the inner sounds and slow ship movements. Work inside holds, tanks and the engine room continues regardless, while exterior deck work is shortened in heavy frost or snow. Where the owner can choose, outside scopes are better planned for the milder months.

faqs.q: What gauging suits a forest-product ship between cargoes?
faqs.a: Hatch covers and coamings, hold plating, frames and the tank-top, because water entering through worn covers or forming as condensation is what wastes these holds. Measuring them between discharge and the next loading, when holds are empty and dry, gives the owner a clear view of whether coamings and covers need repair before the next wet season or survey.
